name: InvestEU Programme
evidence_rating: moderate-thin: Commission interim evaluation with self-reported mobilisation figures; auditors' critique and one causal study concern the predecessor EFSI, not InvestEU itself
summary: InvestEU uses a EUR 26.2 billion EU budget guarantee to unlock more than EUR 372 billion of investment by 2028. The Commission's 2024 mid-term review reported EUR 218 billion expected by end-2023, mostly private, but these are expected rather than realised figures. EU auditors found the predecessor fund overstated its results by 26% and could not prove additionality, although an independent causal study finds its loans did boost firms' investment.

indicators.objective: The 2020 amended proposal's financial statement has no indicators section (1.4.4 is about synergies); monitoring relies on the key performance indicators annexed to the Regulation and guarantee agreements

indicators.indicator: More than EUR 372bn additional public and private investment by 2028 from a EUR 26.2bn EU guarantee (2018 proposal: EUR 650bn from EUR 38bn)
indicators.evidence: Interim evaluation: about EUR 218bn expected to be mobilised by end-2023 (65% private), anticipated multiplier 14.76; 90% of the guarantee allocated, almost 80% of that approved. Figures are expected/approved, not disbursed.

indicators.indicator: Support only investment that would not otherwise happen (market gaps, higher risk)
indicators.evidence: Interim evaluation reports high additionality based on implementing partners' assessments; the Court of Auditors found additionality of the predecessor EFSI insufficiently demonstrated and its mobilised investment overstated by EUR 131bn (26%).

indicators.indicator: Effects on recipient firms' investment, jobs, innovation
indicators.evidence: No causal study of InvestEU yet; a causal study of predecessor EFSI direct loans finds about 12 percentage points extra fixed-asset growth.

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal establishing the InvestEU Programme, SWD(2018) 314
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal establishing the InvestEU Programme
literature.method: ex-ante (builds on EFSI and financial instrument evaluations)
literature.headline: Single EU guarantee of EUR 38bn expected to mobilise EUR 650bn of investment, with a more cautious multiplier than EFSI because of riskier, policy-targeted products; EFSI multiplier 13.5 at end-2017 against a target of 15
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected merging EU investment instruments into one guarantee programme to unlock EUR 650 billion of investment; the final, smaller programme targets EUR 372 billion.
literature.quality: forecast for original 2018 proposal; budget later reduced

literature.citation: European Commission (based on ICF study) (2024), Interim evaluation of the InvestEU Programme, SWD(2024) 228 (executive summary SWD(2024) 229)
literature.title: Interim evaluation of the InvestEU Programme
literature.method: interim evaluation (portfolio data to end-2023, interviews, surveys)
literature.headline: About EUR 218bn expected to be mobilised by end-2023 (65% private), anticipated multiplier 14.76; 90% of the EUR 26.2bn guarantee allocated; meaningful crowding-in and high additionality; budget insufficient relative to demand
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's mid-term review says InvestEU was on track to unlock EUR 218 billion of investment by end-2023, most of it private, and that demand exceeds its budget.
literature.quality: self-evaluation; mobilisation figures are expected, not realised; no counterfactual
literature.verified: page summary (Commission page and press report)

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2025), The European Fund for Strategic Investments: contributed substantially to addressing the investment gap, but had not fully reached the EUR 500 billion target in the real economy by the end of 2022, ECA Special Report 07/2025
literature.title: The European Fund for Strategic Investments: contributed substantially to addressing the investment gap, but had not fully reached the EUR 500 billion target in the real economy by the end of 2022
literature.headline: EFSI contributed substantially to closing the investment gap, but its reported EUR 503bn of mobilised investment was overstated by EUR 131bn (26%) against the EUR 500bn target (undisbursed financing counted, double counting with other EU instruments, cancellations not deducted); additionality not sufficiently demonstrated; no ex-post check of additionality
literature.summary_plain: The EU's auditors found that InvestEU's predecessor overstated the investment it unlocked by about a quarter and could not prove it funded projects that would not have happened anyway, a warning for how InvestEU's figures are read.
literature.quality: audit of predecessor programme, same methodology lineage
literature.verified: abstract read (ECA press release and report contents)

literature.citation: Frayman (2026), The European Fund for Strategic Investments (EFSI): causal effects of a state lending policy, Journal of Economic Policy Reform
literature.title: The European Fund for Strategic Investments (EFSI): causal effects of a state lending policy
literature.headline: EFSI-backed direct EIB loans raised recipients' fixed-asset growth by about 12 percentage points on average after treatment
literature.summary_plain: A causal study of InvestEU's predecessor finds firms receiving its loans grew their fixed assets about 12 percentage points faster than similar firms.
literature.quality: predecessor programme; direct loans, not guarantees
literature.verified: page summary via search (Crossref metadata confirmed)

literature.authors: Bertoni, F., Colombo, M.G., Quas, A.
literature.title: Economic impact assessment of the COSME Loan Guarantee Facility: evidence from Belgium, France and Italy
literature.method: difference-in-differences with propensity-score matching on firm accounts (3 years after signature), fixed-effects panel models, probit and Cox survival models
literature.outcomes: SME growth in assets, sales, employment, fixed assets; labour productivity; survival
literature.headline: Three years after the guaranteed loan, beneficiaries grew 8.0 pp more in assets, 5.4 pp in sales and 7.8 pp in employment than matched firms (all p<0.01), with labour productivity about 2% lower.
literature.summary_plain: Small firms in Belgium, France and Italy that got bank loans backed by the EU's COSME guarantee grew faster in jobs, sales and investment than similar firms without one. The scheme is the direct predecessor of the InvestEU SME guarantee.
literature.quality: Strong matched DiD on predecessor instrument (COSME LGF, now run under InvestEU's SME window); selection on unobservables possible
literature.interested_party: Published by the EIF, which manages the guarantees
literature.citation: Bertoni, F., Colombo, M.G., Quas, A. (2025), Economic impact assessment of the COSME Loan Guarantee Facility: evidence from Belgium, France and Italy, EIF Impact Assessment Working Paper 2025/107

literature.authors: Bertoni, F., Colombo, M.G., Quas, A.
literature.title: Economic impact assessment of the COSME Loan Guarantee Facility: evidence from Greece, Poland, Spain and Romania
literature.method: difference-in-differences with propensity-score matching on firm accounts, fixed-effects panel models, probit and Cox survival models
literature.outcomes: SME growth in assets, sales, employment, fixed assets; productivity; bankruptcy
literature.headline: Beneficiaries outgrew matched firms by 13.3 pp in assets, 10.8 pp in sales and 9.2 pp in employment after three years, with no productivity change, and were 2.8 pp less likely to go bankrupt by end-2023.
literature.summary_plain: In Greece, Poland, Spain and Romania, small firms with EU-guaranteed loans grew faster and were less likely to fail than comparable firms. This is evidence on the guarantee scheme that InvestEU continues.
literature.quality: Strong matched DiD on predecessor instrument (COSME LGF); unobserved selection possible
literature.interested_party: Published by the EIF, which manages the guarantees
literature.citation: Bertoni, F., Colombo, M.G., Quas, A. (2025), Economic impact assessment of the COSME Loan Guarantee Facility: evidence from Greece, Poland, Spain and Romania, EIF Impact Assessment Working Paper 2025/103

literature.authors: EIB Operations Evaluation Division (Bernabè, S., Benko, B. et al.; with Ramboll, GDCC, Panteia)
literature.title: Evaluation of the European Fund for Strategic Investments
literature.venue: EIB Operations Evaluation, Thematic Evaluation Report, June 2018
literature.method: mixed-methods evaluation: portfolio data, original survey of Infrastructure and Innovation Window final beneficiaries, Commission survey of SME Window beneficiaries, case studies
literature.outcomes: investment mobilised; additionality (would projects have happened without support)
literature.headline: Surveys found 76% of SME-window and 67% of infrastructure-window operations would have stopped, shrunk or been delayed without EFSI-backed financing (81% for equity-type vs 63% for debt), and 98% of surveyed debt operations received inputs the market could not provide.
literature.summary_plain: The EIB's own evaluators found that most projects backed by the Juncker Plan guarantee, InvestEU's predecessor, said they would have been smaller, later or cancelled without it.
literature.quality: Predecessor (EFSI) evidence; self-reported counterfactual from beneficiary surveys, likely upward-biased; in-house evaluation
literature.citation: EIB Operations Evaluation Division (Bernabè, S., Benko, B. et al.; with Ramboll, GDCC, Panteia) (2018), Evaluation of the European Fund for Strategic Investments, EIB Operations Evaluation, Thematic Evaluation Report, June 2018
